NEW UNDERCOVER INVESTIGATION: I spent several months investigating a nationwide network of advocacy organizations and medical providers helping families continue medically transitioning their children in defiance of state laws. My investigation centers on Campaign for Southern Equality (CSE), an LGBT advocacy nonprofit that connects families with cooperating medical providers across the country. CSE has distributed over $1 million in travel grants to more than 1,200 families, plus another $1 million to partner organizations, including funding for medical appointments. With CSE's knowledge, providers in its referral network told me the ways that they circumvent state restrictions on gender-transition treatments for minors. Some discussed using alternative diagnosis codes, such as “endocrine disorder,” to facilitate prescriptions or insurance coverage. Others described mailing medications directly to families' homes or sending prescriptions to pharmacies in states where these interventions are banned. Providers also discussed conducting virtual appointments with patients in those states. Others required patients to cross state lines for telehealth but did not appear to have a reliable method for verifying their physical location. My primary undercover scenario involved an 11-year-old girl in Tennessee who had only recently begun identifying as nonbinary, with no long history of gender-related distress. The providers I shared this scenario with seemed eager to treat her. Many indicated that puberty blockers could be prescribed after an initial evaluation lasting just one to several hours. My investigation uncovered practices that may violate state and federal laws and pose medical risks to children living hundreds or thousands of miles from their treating physicians. Read my full @CityJournal investigation: https://www.city-journal.org/article/pediatric-gender-transition-treatments-bans

Today we're launching @snaptrude Agent, the most advanced agent for building design. It does real design work with you, from a site to a construction-ready LOD 400 model with structure, MEP and drawings. Then can go back to your existing software with your families intact. About a year ago we bet the company on AI. Honestly the insight came from software engineering. It wasn't long ago that autocomplete felt like a big deal, and now engineers direct agents that write a lot of the code. I think the same shift is coming to how we design buildings, and it's already started. Most designers I meet aren't short on skill, they're short on time. Take the call every design team dreads, the client cuts the budget by 30%. Today that's a bad month for everyone. With the agent you're the director. You decide where the cost comes out, and it updates the layout, coordinates the structure and MEP, and redoes the drawings. So when design exploration gets this cheap, we go from 3 options to 300, and more options means better buildings. Since August our users have gone through more than 140 billion tokens, and firms like Jacobs, Studio+, Kajima, VMDO, Dekker and hundreds of others use Snaptrude today. In our early access, more than 2,000 designers have run over 25,000 tasks through the agent since September. We also built a benchmark for this, AECBench, because in AEC an almost correct answer is still wrong. It gives AI the same brief an architect would get, has its design in a real BIM model, and scores the result against the brief and against how architects review design. We're publishing the first results today, link below. Thank you @prashanthp at @Accel and Shub and the team at @foundamental for backing us when this was still a bet, and the Snaptrude team, who built every bit of this. Really proud of you all. Thanks to our investors, @scottbelsky, @andreasklinger, @thilokonzok, @immad, @CindyXBi, @DanilaVladi, @jmwass, rahulchaudhary, @adamecourt, Zach Ginsburg, Alex duff, Paul grossinger, really appreciate all the help along the way. Don't sleep on decision models if you build RAG systems. Here is a great new paper on the topic. (bookmark it) It's well known that retrieval is often the weakest step in a RAG pipeline. Generators keep getting stronger while retrievers still match keywords or fixed embeddings. This matters because anything the retriever misses never reaches the generator. This work replaces the retriever with a decision model that walks the corpus from broad topics down to documents and then passages. At each level, DecisionRAG scores every candidate in one forward pass, without generating tokens, and keeps only the most promising branches. With no first-stage retriever and no task-specific training, it beats dense retrieval plus an 8B reranker by 13.8 R@1 points on MultiDoc2Dial and 17.4 Hit@1 points on Natural Questions, where it searches 2.68 million Wikipedia paragraphs. Retrieval takes 0.7 to 1.8 seconds and 0.2 to 2.3 cents per query. Scoring candidates together in one shared context adds up to 7.7 points over judging them one at a time. A Qwen3-8B judge trained on in-domain data reaches 60.7 R@1 on MultiDoc2Dial, 5.7 points above the best published task-trained retriever. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35868 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/retriever-free-retrieval-navigating-documents-with-decision-models-2610.35868

I think “sell picks and shovels” is the wrong lesson for AI startups. The Gold Rush analogy is weaker than the Industrial Revolution. Gold is a single pile that runs out. Machines keep making everything cheaper. Far more people got rich using the new machines than building them.

For every Boulton & Watt (steam engine makers, think NVIDIA in today’s market) there were a hundred firms with names like General Amalgamated Hosiery Corporation that did at least as well. The opposite of Gold Rush dynamics.

And not every massive productivity gain from new technologies in the Industrial Revolution took decades to appear, despite the electricity analogy. https://x.com/emollick/status/2092826292345331773?a=o2eCrL99lTeK-C9pRTo&s=20 I hear the story about how it took 30 years to gain productivity from electricity a lot in relation to AI (I have even told it myself) But not every technology is that way. Ford went from inventing the assembly line to full deployment in 3 years, cutting car building time by 88%
